description: The decision corpus for standards/070-rbac.md — the artifact that makes a polyglot authorization standard enforceable from one source. An implementation loads 'roles', 'scopeContainment' and 'grants', then evaluates every case in 'checks' and either reproduces each expected decision or names the case it failed. Every check states the 'activeGrant' it is made in: a session acts in exactly one grant and the effective permission set is that grant's role's set, so the active grant is an argument like the subject, the permission and the scope (RB5, RB6). No running service and no network: the corpus is data and check() is a pure function of its arguments, which is what RB7 requires and why it requires it. A denied check states the 'denial' it expects, one of the six reasons RB8 names, and an implementation reproduces that too.

scopeContainment.description: The application declares its own hierarchy; this fixture uses one tenant containing two projects, plus a second tenant that contains neither. 'global' contains everything.

checks.note: the base case
viewer does not carry it, and no grant means deny — never 'allow unless denied' (RB6)
the active grant at a containing scope satisfies a check at a contained one, and the reason names the scope the grant is actually held at (RB5)
usr_ben acts in approver on one project only; a project grant does not reach the tenant. The inverse of the case above, and the one an implementation gets wrong by treating containment as symmetric
alpha and beta share a tenant; a grant on one reaches neither the other nor their parent
usr_cara acts in tenant_admin of acme and holds nothing at all in globex

THE SCOPE CACHE CASE, and the reason it is in the corpus rather than left to review. Evaluate 'before' first, then the check: an implementation whose cache keys on subject and permission without scope returns allowed for both and fails here. That is a cross-tenant authorization result produced by a cache key, and no test exercising one tenant at a time will ever show it (RB7, RB9)
a global grant reaches everywhere, including a tenant the subject has no other relationship with
global is a scope, not a superuser. auditor carries report permissions and nothing else, wherever it is held

THE ROLE-NAME CASE, and the mechanical detector for RB4. usr_fay acts in regional_auditor, a tenant-defined role carrying exactly the permissions of the code-declared auditor. An implementation that gates on a role name — 'is this subject an auditor' — refuses a subject the permission model plainly allows, and fails here while passing every other case. It is also why fixture roles carry an 'origin': the corpus has to be able to express a role the code never heard of

THE ONE-ACTIVE-GRANT CASE, and the one that separates this model from an additive one. usr_eve holds viewer and approver at the same scope and is acting in viewer. Grants are never combined, so the effective permission set is viewer's set and approver's invoice.approve is not in it. An implementation that unions every grant that applies returns allowed here and fails (RB6)

THE GRANT CACHE CASE. Evaluate 'before' first, then the check: same subject, same permission, same scope, and a different active grant. An implementation whose cache key omits the active grant returns the denial again and fails here. That is the RB9 key stated as a case, and it is the defect a change of active grant introduces (RB9)
neither viewer nor approver carries invoice.void, so the answer is deny whichever of the two usr_eve is acting in
approver holds invoice.read explicitly. It is in the corpus to make the converse observable: approve does not imply read, and read is granted here only because the role lists it (RB6)
a subject with no grants at all, and so no active grant to act in. Distinct from 060-auth.md AU6's unknown subject, which never reaches a check

viewer's set, sorted, complete, and not a union with the approver grant usr_eve also holds. This is what feeds the /me document of 060-auth.md AU6, and it is why RB6 forbids a wildcard surviving into the check: a subject holding one would have every permission while this list enumerated none of them, and the interface would render the wrong screen
the same subject at the same scope, acting in the other grant. The pair states RB6 as data: the answer is the active role's set and never the union of the two
empty rather than absent — 'this subject can do nothing here' is a statement, not a missing answer
usr_ana holds the first and not the second
a codebase without checkAny and checkAll writes the loop by hand and gets it wrong somewhere, which is why RB7 declares both
an empty list is a call site that forgot to say what it was checking, and a guard that allows everything it is put in front of is not a guard (RB7)
every permission in an empty list is held, so the naive loop allows; the refusal is what the caller can see (RB7)

rejections.stimulus: store a role whose permissions include 'invoice.aprove'
rejections.note: validated at write time (RB3). Accepted silently, it grants nothing and says nothing, and surfaces later as a person who cannot do what everyone believes they can
a resource that has not been named; it is system_dashboard.view (RB2)

rejections.stimulus: declare, store, check against, or offer as authoring shorthand any of '*', 'system.*' or 'invoice.*'
rejections.note: the rule with the most evidence behind it, and a flat denial rather than a check-time one. A wildcard surviving into the check silently defeats every other rule and makes permissionsFor untrue; a wildcard admitted as authoring shorthand either re-expands and silently grows or freezes and silently stops meaning what it says. There is no place in the system where one is accepted (RB6)
an error, not a denial. A denial is indistinguishable from a correct refusal and hides the typo forever (RB1). The decision returned beside the error carries the reason (RB8)

rejections.stimulus: as a tenant administrator, edit the permissions of a code-declared system role, then attempt to delete it
rejections.note: the recovery floor. If every administrative role is data, deleting them locks everyone out with no path back that does not involve raw SQL against production (RB3)

rejections.stimulus: create a tenant-defined role named the same as an existing system role
rejections.note: a lookup by name must have one answer. Shadowing is also how a tenant would otherwise redefine a role the code refers to by name (RB3)

rejections.stimulus: create a tenant-defined role containing a permission string that is well-formed but not in the application's declared set
rejections.note: this is the check that makes runtime roles safe at all. A role composes capabilities that already exist and are already enforced; the closed permission set of RB1 is exactly what bounds a role's blast radius, so relaxing RB1 would make RB3 indefensible with it

rejections.stimulus: in a product whose Conventions declare a single grant per subject, write a second grant for a subject that already holds one
rejections.note: whether a subject holds more than one grant is a product choice declared in Conventions (RB5). Where the product declares one, the second grant is refused at write time rather than left for a session to choose between. A subject holding two grants in a product that admits one has no defined active grant, and the choice of capacity stops being the person's

rejections.stimulus: call check() with the scope 'acme' (neither global nor type:id)
rejections.note: a scope that is not a scope is the same mistake as an undeclared permission: an error about the call, never a denial about the person (RB5, RB8)

rejections.stimulus: declare the scope 'global:acme' and grant a role at it
rejections.note: 'global:acme' is a scope of type 'global' and model.schema.json's pattern admits it; an implementation is never stricter than the schema, because a shape one module refuses and another accepts is the divergence one schema exists to prevent (RB5)
